Inside an experiment

Preprint forthcoming · 2026

Less output.
How much reasoning?

Can silent placeholders replace visible chain-of-thought? My study tests prompted latent reasoning across 13,000 model calls, 5 models and 5 datasets.

Read the findings ↓
−6.8pp

The trade-off matters.

Overall accuracy trails chain-of-thought by 6.8 absolute percentage points. Results vary by task; arithmetic still benefits from explicit reasoning.

Study abstract, scope & key findings +

Can Silent Placeholders Replace Chain-of-Thought? A Token-Efficiency Study of Prompted Latent Reasoning

Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting improves reasoning accuracy by making models emit intermediate natural-language steps, but these visible traces can dominate output length and latency. We study a lightweight alternative: prompted latent reasoning, where a model receives a short sequence of placeholder slots such as <latent_1> and is instructed to use them internally while emitting only the final answer. This mechanism does not train new latent tokens; instead, it tests whether existing instruction-tuned local models can approximate silent reasoning through prompting alone. Across 13,000 de-duplicated model calls on five reasoning datasets, latent prompting reduces visible output tokens by 93.5% and latency by 88.7% relative to CoT, while trailing CoT by only 6.8 absolute accuracy points overall. The trade-off is strongly task-dependent: CoT remains essential for arithmetic, while latent prompting matches or exceeds CoT on ARC-Challenge and PrOntoQA-style tasks.

  • 93.5% reduction in visible output tokens vs. CoT across 5 models and 5 datasets
  • 88.7% latency reduction with only 6.8pp accuracy drop overall
  • Latent prompting matches or exceeds CoT on ARC-Challenge and PrOntoQA-style tasks
  • CoT remains essential for arithmetic; latent prompting is a strong inference-time baseline for other task types

The person behind the questions

Structure over
shortcuts.

Venkat Chavan N
MSc Big Data & AI
SRH University, BerlinDownload CV ↗

My work asks when a model learns structure, and when it takes a shortcut. I explore this through retrieval-grounded systems, linguistic benchmarks and coordinated learning.

My research agenda +

My long-term research goal is to develop AI systems that are not only accurate, but also interpretable, evidence-grounded, and robust under distribution shift. Across my work, I am interested in the gap between pattern recognition and reasoning: when does a model truly learn structure, and when is it exploiting shortcuts in data?

My recent projects approach this question from multiple directions: hierarchical RAG for cyber threat intelligence, benchmark design for Sanskrit linguistic generalisation, neuro-symbolic biomedical reasoning, and coordinated multi-agent learning for autonomous driving. A common theme across these projects is evaluation: building systems whose outputs can be traced, tested, compared, and challenged.

I am particularly interested in PhD and research roles involving trustworthy LLMs, neuro-symbolic AI, retrieval-augmented generation, multi-agent learning, causal representation learning, and AI evaluation methodology.

Five connected research interests +

Trustworthy LLM Systems

Hallucination control, evidence grounding, RAG evaluation, citation accuracy, and adversarial robustness of retrieval-augmented language models.

Neuro-Symbolic AI & Structured Reasoning

Knowledge graphs, symbolic constraints, rule-based reasoning, and structured representations as a route to reasoning beyond surface-level pattern matching.

Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

Coordinated autonomous driving in mixed-traffic environments, zero-shot transfer, safety-rule evaluation, and GNN/GAT-enhanced agent coordination.

Language Model Evaluation

SanskritEval, sandhi segmentation, morphological generalisation, low-resource NLP, and benchmark design that separates linguistic structure from surface patterns.

Privacy-Preserving & Security-Aware AI

Encrypted vector operations, privacy-preserving retrieval, cyber threat intelligence, defensive AI tooling, and PII-aware evidence handling.
